desc: With this Galileo's Paradox of Infinity calculator, you'll be able to understand Galileo's paradox of infinity and how to compare infinite sets!

c: Galileo, logically, considered that the number of perfect squares must be less than the number of naturals (non-negative integers). Let's see why: Input any two numbers and see how many natural numbers and perfect square numbers are between them.

There {{isare.value}} {{nSquares.value}} {{perfect.value}} and {{nNats.value}} {{natural.value}} between {{lower.value}} and {{greater.value}}. Set of perfect squares: {{message3.valueMarkdown}} Set of natural numbers: {{message5.valueMarkdown}}

Apparently, there are more natural numbers than squares in any range we choose. But... At the same time, he considered that there cannot be more integers than squares, since: "... each root has its own square and each square its root." This means that for every natural number, a single square exists (its square), and that for every square there is exactly one natural number that corresponds to it.

So, what did Galileo take away from this paradox? He concluded that the notions of "greater", "less", and "equal" should apply only to finite quantities. However, we now know that these notions are applicable to any two sets in terms of their "cardinality" and the one-to-one correspondence between their elements.
We can then introduce the following definition: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection (one-to-one correspondence) from A to B.
According to this definition, if we compare the set of integers: ℤ = {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...} and the set of natural numbers including 0: ℕ = {0, 1, 2, ...}

✔️ Correct! There exists a one-to-one correspondence between both sets, therefore, integers and naturals have the same cardinality. One possible bijection is: g(n) = (n + 1) / 2, if n is odd g(n) = -n / 2, if n is even
